Description: The Tarteaucitron library fails to properly validate the data-cookie attribute within its cookie consent management functionality. This vulnerability stems from an insecure client-side implementation that allows external influence over internal cookie removal operations. An attacker can leverage this flaw to delete arbitrary cookies, potentially disrupting session state or security controls for authenticated users.
PoC: An unauthenticated attacker crafts a malicious web link targeting a user's browser. The attacker directs the user to trigger a Tarteaucitron configuration that includes a crafted data-cookie attribute. The victim's browser executes the deletion logic while processing the malformed attribute provided by the attacker. This results in the removal of the targeted application cookies from the victim's local browser environment.

Finding_Name: CPU DoS in Libp2p Control Messages
Description: The libp2p library contains a denial-of-service vulnerability within its control message handling for IHAVE and IWANT arrays. The root cause is an insufficient validation of message array sizes, allowing oversized packets to exhaust CPU resources during processing. This vulnerability permits an unauthenticated remote attacker to trigger resource exhaustion, causing an application-level denial of service.
PoC: An unauthenticated remote attacker sends a specifically crafted series of IHAVE and IWANT gossipsub messages to the libp2p node. The node attempts to parse these oversized arrays without implementing strict size limits or memory allocation bounds. The CPU enters an infinite or high-latency loop while attempting to iterate through the malicious structures. This results in the service becoming unresponsive to legitimate network traffic.

Finding_Name: SSRF in Kimai PDF Invoice Rendering
Description: Kimai is vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery via the invoice PDF rendering component that processes Markdown image URLs. The flaw exists due to an lack of input validation or allow-listing of requested URLs before the server attempts to fetch the remote content. An unauthenticated attacker can exploit this to force the server to perform requests to internal resources, compromising network segmentation.
PoC: An unauthenticated remote attacker identifies the invoice generation endpoint in Kimai that supports Markdown image embedding. The attacker submits a PDF generation request with an image URL set to an internal service, such as a local metadata service at 169.254.169.254. The server-side rendering engine attempts to fetch the URL, retrieving sensitive information that the attacker can extract from the generated document. This results in unauthorized access to internal network metadata and services.

Description: The morgan logging middleware is vulnerable to log forging due to unneutralized control characters in the :remote-user logging token. This issue arises because the input is reflected directly into logs without sanitizing CR/LF characters, allowing for arbitrary log entry manipulation. An attacker can exploit this to inject malicious data into log files, potentially deceiving administrators or interfering with automated monitoring tools.
PoC: An unauthenticated attacker sends a HTTP request with a specially crafted user-agent or header value that populates the :remote-user token with newline and carriage return characters. The morgan middleware processes this input and writes a new, fabricated log entry to the server-side log file. The server logs now contain malicious data that mimics system alerts or hides the attacker's actual activities. This results in the compromise of log integrity and audit traceability.

Finding_Name: Cross-User Attribute Leak in API Platform
Description: API Platform Core suffers from a cross-user attribute leak in JSON:API and HAL normalizers due to a missing isCacheKeySafe gate. This failure to validate the cache context allows data cached by one user to be served to another user, leading to unauthorized information disclosure. This vulnerability requires a specific configuration where data is cached using an unsafe key, potentially exposing sensitive data to unauthorized parties.
PoC: An attacker monitors the application to identify frequently requested items served by the API Platform normalizers. The attacker induces a cache population with sensitive attribute data using their own session. A second victim user then requests the same resource, at which point the server retrieves the attacker-poisoned cache entry. This results in the leakage of sensitive user-specific attributes to unauthorized third parties.

Description: The Tesla framework is susceptible to multipart part smuggling due to improper sanitization of content-disposition values. The technical root cause is the failure to escape special characters within the header, enabling attackers to inject additional parts into the multipart message. This can be exploited by an unauthenticated attacker to bypass downstream filtering or confuse the parsing logic of receiving services.
PoC: An unauthenticated attacker constructs a malicious HTTP request utilizing the Tesla framework's multipart parsing logic. The attacker includes a specially crafted content-disposition header that introduces unintended boundaries or field components. The framework interprets the input incorrectly, smuggling a hidden part into the message body. This results in successful bypass of security validations applied only to the initial legitimate part.

Description: Tesla is vulnerable to atom exhaustion via the processing of untrusted URL schemes, which may trigger excessive resource consumption during parsing. The root cause is a lack of limit on the number of entities processed, allowing an attacker to force the framework into a state of resource exhaustion. This can lead to a denial-of-service condition where the server stops responding to legitimate requests.
PoC: An unauthenticated attacker sends a high volume of requests to the Tesla framework that triggers the parsing of deep or recursive URL-based atom structures. The internal parser attempts to allocate memory or compute resources for each nested atom without appropriate bounds enforcement. The server's available memory or CPU capacity is depleted by the recursive requests. This results in an application-level denial of service for all users.

Description: The Tesla framework incorrectly handles Authorization headers during cross-origin redirects due to case-sensitive filtering. This vulnerability allows the sensitive credentials to be leaked to third-party endpoints if the redirect target's case differs from the filter expectation. An attacker can capture these headers, facilitating further unauthorized access to protected resources.
PoC: An unauthenticated attacker orchestrates a cross-origin redirect by controlling the destination of an application request. The attacker sets the redirection domain to a controlled server and manipulates the casing of the header filter to allow the Authorization header to pass through. The browser or framework transmits the valid Authorization header to the attacker-controlled server upon redirection. This results in the theft of authentication tokens for the victim's session.

Description: Tesla is susceptible to a decompression bomb attack where a maliciously small compressed response body results in massive memory allocation. The vulnerability occurs because the framework fails to enforce ratio-based limits on decompression, allowing malicious payloads to trigger excessive system resource use. An unauthenticated attacker can effectively crash the service through memory exhaustion.
PoC: An unauthenticated attacker sends a request to a Tesla-powered service that triggers a response containing an highly compressed data object. The attacker crafts the compressed object so that its expansion creates a stream of data exceeding available system memory. The server's decompression process attempts to fulfill the memory request, leading to an immediate OOM (Out-of-Memory) crash. This results in the complete unavailability of the affected service.

Description: The Tesla framework contains a CRLF injection vulnerability within the request `Content-Type` header processing. This occurs because the `add_content_type_param` function fails to sanitize user-supplied input before embedding it into the header string. An attacker can inject CRLF characters to terminate the current header and begin injecting malicious headers or request body content.
PoC: An unauthenticated attacker sends an HTTP request where the `Content-Type` parameter includes encoded CRLF characters. The Tesla framework's `add_content_type_param` function parses the input and inserts the characters into the header structure of the generated outbound request. This results in the ability to poison downstream caches or perform HTTP Request Smuggling against secondary systems.

Description: The Mistune library is vulnerable to a denial-of-service condition due to quadratic-time complexity in its parse_link_text function. The root cause is the inefficient handling of link text pattern matching when processing deeply nested or complex Markdown constructs. An attacker can supply a specially crafted input to trigger extreme CPU consumption, effectively stalling the parsing service.
PoC: An unauthenticated attacker submits a large Markdown text input containing an intentionally complex chain of nested links and formatting patterns to the application's input processing field. The Mistune engine's `parse_link_text` function enters a quadratic processing loop while trying to resolve the syntax. The server resource utilization spikes to 100%, causing the application to hang or timeout. This results in a widespread service degradation or complete denial of service for all users.

Description: GoBGP is vulnerable to a service crash during confederation validation when encountering an empty AS_PATH attribute. The technical root cause is an unhandled case or nil pointer dereference within the BGP attribute parsing logic. An unauthenticated attacker can exploit this via malicious BGP peer communication to cause the GoBGP daemon to terminate unexpectedly.
PoC: An unauthenticated attacker establishes a BGP connection to a GoBGP daemon peer. The attacker sends a BGP UPDATE message that omits the AS_PATH attribute in a confederation-enabled session. The GoBGP parsing logic fails to validate the presence of the required path data and triggers a runtime panic during attribute verification. This results in the GoBGP service crashing and losing connectivity to all active BGP peers.

Finding_Name: OOB Read in GoBGP Capability Parser
Description: GoBGP is vulnerable to an out-of-bounds read in its BGP OPEN capability parser when reading values exceeding declared CapLen boundaries. This vulnerability occurs due to insufficient length checks, allowing an attacker to read adjacent memory in the heap. This may lead to information disclosure if sensitive memory content is returned in error messages or protocol exchanges.
PoC: An unauthenticated attacker initiates a BGP connection to a GoBGP target. The attacker crafts a BGP OPEN message containing a capability field with a CapLen value that does not match the actual length of the payload, causing the parser to read past the end of the intended data. The GoBGP process inadvertently reads out-of-bounds heap memory and returns portions of it in subsequent communication. This results in the potential leak of sensitive internal memory contents to the remote attacker.

Description: The psd-tools library is vulnerable to arbitrary file write via path traversal in the smart-object filename parsing. The technical root cause is the failure to sanitize file paths extracted from the PSD metadata, allowing relative path segments to escape the intended write directory. A malicious PSD file can be used by an attacker to overwrite arbitrary files on the local filesystem.
PoC: An unauthenticated attacker sends a malicious PSD file containing a smart-object with a name set to '../../../../etc/passwd' or similar system path to a target user. The victim opens the file using an application leveraging psd-tools for processing. The library attempts to save the smart-object data to the specified location, writing the attacker-controlled content to the target file path. This results in a full system compromise via file overwriting.

Description: The sigstore-go library has a multi-log threshold bypass vulnerability when verifying log records. The failure to correctly validate consistency across all required logs allows a single compromised log server to satisfy the entire threshold verification process. This compromises the integrity of signed artifacts if an attacker compromises one of the involved logs.
PoC: An attacker compromises a single log server that is part of a multi-log threshold verification scheme. The attacker submits a malicious artifact metadata payload to the compromised log. The sigstore-go verification client accepts the single compromised log's signature as sufficient proof of artifact legitimacy, bypassing the requirement for cross-log verification. This results in the successful deployment or execution of unauthorized, unverified software artifacts.

Description: Rattler is vulnerable to path traversal within the package cache during the construction of file paths from build strings. The root cause is the failure to validate the conda package build string, which can contain path separators to escape the target directory. An attacker can provide a malicious package build string to write or read arbitrary files on the local filesystem.
PoC: An unauthenticated attacker hosts a malicious package repository that provides a crafted build string. The victim pulls this package using the Rattler client. The client attempts to cache the package and resolves a path containing '../' segments from the build string. This results in the package contents being written outside the intended cache directory, allowing for arbitrary file modification on the victim's system.

Description: OpenRun is vulnerable to an open redirect due to improper validation of redirect URLs involving absolute paths or host identifiers. The technical root cause is a failure in the URL parsing logic to distinguish between local resource paths and malicious external hosts. An attacker can exploit this to redirect users to unauthorized, potentially malicious websites, facilitating phishing attacks.
PoC: An attacker creates a malicious URL that uses the //host pattern to point to an external site. The attacker sends this URL as a parameter to the OpenRun redirection endpoint. The application processes the URL without adequate validation of the host component. The user is redirected to the attacker-controlled site, potentially leading to credential harvesting or malware delivery.

Description: The mint HTTP/2 implementation is vulnerable to a denial-of-service attack via unbounded stream map growth caused by PUSH_PROMISE frames that lack a follow-up HEADERS frame. The technical root cause is a failure to enforce timeouts or resource limits for streams created via PUSH_PROMISE. An attacker can flood the server with these frames to exhaust system memory.
PoC: An unauthenticated remote attacker initiates an HTTP/2 connection to a Mint-powered server. The attacker sends a high volume of PUSH_PROMISE frames without sending any corresponding HEADERS frames. The server creates internal state for each pending stream, which remains open indefinitely. The server's memory is exhausted, resulting in a denial-of-service condition for all legitimate incoming requests.

Description: The mint library is vulnerable to a denial-of-service via unbounded CONTINUATION/HEADERS frame accumulation. The root cause is the failure to limit the number of continuation frames allowed per request, allowing an attacker to hold connections open and consume server resources. This leads to connection starvation and service downtime.
PoC: An unauthenticated remote attacker sends a large series of HTTP/2 CONTINUATION frames to a Mint-enabled web server without completing the request. The Mint library processes each frame and keeps the connection state active while waiting for more data. The server's available connection slots and CPU time are consumed, preventing new requests from being serviced. This results in a persistent denial-of-service condition.

Description: The mint library accepts a non-RFC compliant '+' sign prefix in the Content-Length header, leading to potential request smuggling. This vulnerability arises from lax parsing logic that ignores deviations from the specification, potentially creating a desynchronization between different middlebox security filters. An attacker can leverage this discrepancy to bypass security controls implemented on the edge.
PoC: An unauthenticated attacker sends an HTTP request using a `Content-Length` header with a leading '+' sign (e.g., `+100`). The Mint server parses the value correctly and proceeds with request handling, while a front-end load balancer may reject it or treat it as zero-length. This discrepancy allows the attacker to inject malicious requests that are processed by the back-end application but ignored by the security filter. This results in successful HTTP request smuggling or bypass of WAF protections.
